title: Time, priorities and a workable plan
provenance: Original fictional practice commissioned for this curriculum; not authentic IELTS, not standardised or score-calibrated. No third-party text or diagrams used.

word_count_method: Regex word tokens including hyphenated forms; excludes speaker labels, titles, question text and Q locators.

planning_only.note: Text-based estimate only. Future rendition must fit 32 minutes including part pauses; if not, revise the timetable before release.

tasks.task: Future continuous first listen, including planned part pauses
Submit first answers and confidence, without a second play
Four Q-located intensive segments, 15 minutes each

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Learning hub bookings, good morning.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Hello. I'd like to join one of your short workshops, but the list includes several kinds of planning. I'm not looking for advice about choosing a career. I need help organising a small project with a deadline.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Then project planning is the relevant workshop.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Yes, please record project planning as my main interest. I can usually begin a task, but I sometimes spend too much time on the first section and leave the final checks unfinished.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: The introduction looks at how to identify required work and divide the available time, including decisions about what to do when a stage takes longer than expected.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Which date were you considering?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: My colleague mentioned the eleventh of March, although I think she saw an early notice.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: That was the provisional date. The confirmed workshop is on the eighteenth of March.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The eighteenth is possible for us. I'll replace the earlier message in our group folder so people don't keep returning to it.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Thank you. We will repeat the date in your confirmation.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll use that message when arranging the visit. A corrected date in one conversation can easily be missed if the calendar entry still comes from an older notice, especially when several people are making their own travel plans.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: What time does the workshop start?

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Ten forty in the morning. The hub opens at ten, but the first forty minutes are used for other arrivals and room preparation.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Then ten forty is the time for our session, not ten o'clock.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Correct. Please arrive shortly before the workshop so you can check in without missing the introduction.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll put the session time and the suggested arrival separately in our message.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: That's helpful. Otherwise someone may treat an arrival reminder as the teaching start and become concerned that the leader is late, when the workshop is following exactly the timetable we agreed.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: How many places do you need?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: There are five people involved in our project, but two are unavailable that morning. We need three places.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Three places are available.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Good. The other two can read our notes afterwards, but we won't book seats for them just in case.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: If the confirmed attendance changes, contact us before transferring a place to another person. We need a current list for the room and the introductory activity.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll explain that to the group. It's easier to update one booking properly than to arrive with a different number and expect the leader to redesign the exercise on the spot.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: What is the total charge for those places?

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: The introductory group rate for your three places is thirty-six pounds altogether.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: So thirty-six pounds is the booking total, rather than the price for each participant?

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Exactly. It covers the session materials as well as the three places. Other workshops have different arrangements, so the confirmation will identify this introduction clearly.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll give the total to the person managing our small training budget.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Please check the document before paying. If the number of places or the total doesn't match this conversation, let us correct the record rather than assume that an unexplained difference is an extra service you requested.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Should we bring an unfinished project to work on?

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: You can bring a brief description, but the item we specifically ask for is your current timetable. It helps you see where a proposed plan would fit among existing commitments.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll bring the timetable I actually use, rather than create an ideal week for the exercise.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Good. A current timetable with awkward gaps can be more useful than a neat invented one. We supply the worksheets for the planning task.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll tell the others that a description of the project is optional, while the timetable is the preparation they should definitely complete before the session.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Does the workshop promise that we'll finish every project faster?

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: No. Its purpose is to help you make a clearer allocation and notice where a plan is unrealistic. Sometimes the sensible result is to reduce the task or negotiate a deadline, rather than work more quickly.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: That sounds useful. I don't want our group to treat a planning exercise as proof that any amount of work can fit into an afternoon.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Exactly. You will practise making choices under a stated limit. The value lies in understanding those choices and their consequences, not in claiming that the limit disappears once somebody draws a sufficiently detailed chart.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: One participant finds long written instructions difficult to process in a busy room. Should we mention that now?

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Please describe the practical requirement in your reply to the confirmation. The leader can explain how the instructions are presented and discuss what support is available.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: So we shouldn't simply assume that sitting near the front resolves it.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: That's right. Different people need different arrangements, and we should explain any limits as well as possibilities.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll ask the participant what would help and send that information.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Thank you. That gives us a useful basis for discussion without guessing from a general label or making a promise before we understand the situation.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Can we stay afterwards for individual advice about our whole project?

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: The workshop includes a short group review, but a personal consultation requires a separate booking. The leader cannot guarantee extra time after the session because another group may be waiting.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: We'll prepare one question that fits the workshop review, then enquire separately if we need a longer discussion.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: That's a good approach. The review can help you identify what remains uncertain without becoming an unplanned appointment.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll explain the difference to our colleagues, so they don't bring a large folder expecting somebody to examine every document before we leave.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: If our plans change, which contact route should we use?

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Reply to the booking confirmation with the reference number. That connects the message to the correct workshop and attendance record. A note in the public discussion group may be useful to other participants, but it doesn't update the booking.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll keep the confirmation accessible rather than save only a screenshot of the date.

turns.speaker: Adviser
turns.text: Good. If the change is urgent and the session is close, use the telephone number printed in that message.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Then our group will have one current set of instructions for both attending and making a change, instead of several incomplete versions.

turns.speaker: Hub host
turns.text: Welcome to the learning hub. On the diagram, north is at the top and the entrance is on the southern edge. The lobby is the central reference point. Eight lettered spaces surround it, and their letters do not stand for room names. The welcome desk is directly south of the lobby, on the entrance axis. It isn't in either southern corner. Please check in there before joining an activity. Staff can confirm the room and tell you whether the group is ready. Even if you have attended before, the welcome desk may have information about a revised arrangement that isn't visible on the copy of the plan you brought.

turns.speaker: Hub host
turns.text: The planning studio is in the north-west corner. An earlier room list placed it directly north of the lobby, but that space now serves another purpose. The studio is west of the northern central room and diagonally north-west of the lobby. Today's planning introduction takes place there. Tables are arranged for small groups to compare choices without treating one group's timetable as a model everybody must copy. Please leave bags where the leader indicates so the working surfaces remain available. If you need a different seating arrangement, ask before the task begins rather than moving a table into a position that blocks another group's access to the materials.

turns.speaker: Hub host
turns.text: The individual practice booths are directly east of the lobby, level with its centre. They are not in the south-east room. Participants use them for short tasks that require a quieter setting, under the booking arrangement explained at reception. A booth that appears empty may be reserved for somebody who will arrive shortly, so please don't move in without checking. The booths aren't designed for a group discussion. If a task turns into a conversation with several people, ask staff about an appropriate room. The distinction helps us provide both individual work and collaborative activities without expecting one space to serve incompatible purposes at the same moment.

turns.speaker: Hub host
turns.text: The review room is in the north-east corner, directly north of the practice booths. It is also east of the northern central room, since those two rooms share the same northern row on the diagram. Please use that distinction when explaining its location: being in the north-east corner of the whole map is different from being north-east of the room beside it. The review room supports small-group conversations after a task. Its purpose is to examine decisions and unresolved questions, not simply to announce which person finished first. A useful review can include an unfinished response if the participant can explain how the time was allocated and where the plan broke down.

turns.speaker: Hub host
turns.text: The printing point is in the south-west area. It is west of the welcome desk and below the space directly west of the lobby. Please use the current worksheet version named by your leader. Several activities have similar-looking sheets, and a page left beside the printer may belong to another group. If a printed instruction seems inconsistent with the briefing, ask before beginning rather than quietly choose whichever version you prefer. The printing point is separate from the welcome desk, although staff can direct you if you need help finding it. Mark the south-west letter for this final location, and keep the plan available during the visit rather than relying on memory alone.

turns.speaker: Hub host
turns.text: A timed activity in this hub has a stated purpose. Sometimes the aim is to practise allocating attention; sometimes it is to identify a misunderstanding that remains even with enough time. The leader will explain which kind of task you are doing. Finishing quickly is not automatically evidence of a better response, especially if a required part has been omitted. Equally, taking longer does not prove that someone has thought more carefully. The review considers the response and the decisions behind it. Please avoid turning every timed exercise into a race, because that can change the behaviour the activity was intended to help you notice.

turns.speaker: Hub host
turns.text: When an instruction is unclear, use the clarification procedure before inventing an extra requirement. A participant may spend several minutes making a table because they assume every response needs one, even though the task asks only for a short explanation. Another may omit an essential comparison because the word comparison was overlooked. The useful first step is to identify what the instruction actually requires. The leader can clarify the procedure, but won't make every substantive choice for you. Learning to distinguish a requirement from a preferred style is part of the activity, and the distinction often matters more than adding another attractive feature to an already incomplete answer.

turns.speaker: Hub host
turns.text: The visible timer marks the agreed working period. When it ends, follow the leader's instruction about stopping or marking your current position. Don't quietly continue writing and then describe the whole response as work completed within the original limit. An unfinished sentence can provide useful information about planning, whereas an inaccurate timing record hides the very problem the exercise is meant to reveal. If you need extra time for a separately agreed access arrangement, that arrangement will be recorded clearly. The purpose is an honest account of the conditions under which the work was produced, not a comparison that pretends every participant used an identical procedure when they did not.

turns.speaker: Hub host
turns.text: During group review, explain one allocation decision and its consequence. You might describe why you spent longer checking the task, shortened an example or left a final minute for a required comparison. These are examples of reasoning to discuss, not universal rules for every task. A plan that works for a familiar short response may fail when the information is new or the required output changes. Listen for the condition under which another person's suggestion was useful. Copying the number of minutes without understanding the task can turn a helpful example into a misleading rule, especially when the example comes from a participant with different prior knowledge.

turns.speaker: Hub host
turns.text: Before leaving, record one change you intend to test and the evidence that motivates it. Avoid writing only that you need better time management. That statement is too broad to guide the next attempt. A more useful note identifies a particular stage, such as checking whether both requested outputs are present before polishing the wording. You should also record a feature of your approach that worked well enough to retain. The next session can then compare a deliberate adjustment with the earlier method. This makes the review a link between attempts, rather than a collection of general advice that feels sensible but never changes what happens during the task.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: You've brought the notes from last week's pilot, so let's use them to plan the next session.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: I suggest dividing the working period into short blocks with a specific purpose for each one.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: I resisted that before the pilot because I expected it to interrupt concentration. But our first section expanded until there was no checking time. I'll support blocks if each has a clear task.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Would the lengths be identical for every exercise?

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: No, we'd allocate them after reading the requirements.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: That matters. I'm agreeing to purposeful blocks, not a fixed formula that we apply before we know what the task asks us to produce.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Jade also proposes stopping immediately when each block alarm sounds.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: I favour that for the next practice. Otherwise I'll keep telling myself that one more sentence won't matter.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: I'd allow the person to finish a short unit of thought and then move on. An abrupt stop could leave the later review difficult to follow.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: We could mark the point where the alarm sounded, but I still want an immediate stop in this exercise.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Leo, does marking the point change your preference?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: It would make the timing honest, but I still prefer a brief planned transition.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: Then we disagree about this rule, even though we both support using blocks.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What about a separate buffer at the end?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: I support reserving a small buffer for an unexpected problem. Our last plan allocated every minute before we knew whether the source material would be easy to interpret.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: I'd rather assign all the available time to the required stages and shorten a stage if needed. Otherwise I may treat the buffer as spare time to spend early.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Could a clearly labelled buffer reduce that temptation?

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: Perhaps, but for my next attempt I still prefer the fully allocated plan.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: I continue to favour a reserve. We should test the difference rather than write that everyone needs the same arrangement.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Your draft tracking sheet asks participants to account for every minute. Why?

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: I thought that detail would reveal where time disappeared. Looking at the sheet now, completing it could interrupt the task repeatedly.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: I don't support that level of tracking during the exercise. A few stage markers would be more manageable.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: Agreed. I'll remove the minute-by-minute requirement.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are you abandoning all records?

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: No, just that proposal. We can note stage starts and significant interruptions without narrating every minute.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: That gives us enough information for a useful review.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. Keep the revised decision distinct from the original idea when you write the final procedure.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Should participants estimate the time needed before attempting the task?

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: Yes. Comparing an estimate with actual stage times could show a recurring misunderstanding.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: I agree, provided the estimate is made after reading the requirements, not from the task's page length alone.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What would you do with a large difference?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Ask what happened at the stage concerned. The estimate might be poor, but an unexpected interruption could also explain it.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: So we both support estimating first and reviewing the difference afterwards. We won't call every mismatch a planning failure without looking at the conditions.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: That qualification will make the record more useful than a simple accurate-or-inaccurate label.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Leo suggests repeating any unclear instruction aloud before starting.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: I support that in our paired practice. Hearing my interpretation might reveal that I've missed a required output.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: I'd prefer writing a brief task summary. Reading aloud could become a routine repetition without checking meaning.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Could you ask the partner to explain what they heard?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Yes, that is the version I have in mind.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: It improves the proposal, but I still prefer the written summary for my next attempt.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then Leo supports the spoken check and Jade doesn't. Your different preferences can be tested, but don't report either procedure as agreed by both of you today.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Which two preparation actions have you definitely selected for the shared procedure?

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: First, identify the instruction verbs before dividing the time. A request to compare is different from a request to describe one example.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Agreed. We should connect each verb with the work it requires, rather than just circle it mechanically.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Will participants underline every sentence?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: No, that would hide the important signals among too many marks.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: We also rejected beginning with a decorative introduction before checking the task.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then identifying the instruction verbs is the first agreed action. It helps define the work, but doesn't replace making a decision about how to answer.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: And the second agreed preparation action?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Mark each required output. In the pilot, one person wrote a thoughtful explanation but omitted the requested short recommendation.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: Yes. A small checklist could make that omission visible before the final minute.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are you adding a guess about the participant's eventual score to the preparation sheet?

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: No. That doesn't tell us what the response must contain.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: The two selected actions are identifying instruction verbs and marking required outputs.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. Keep the list short enough to use. A preparation routine that consumes most of the working period can create another problem even if every individual step sounds useful in isolation.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What two limitations must appear in your account of last week's pilot?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: First, it covered only one afternoon. We don't know whether the same allocation problems would occur at another time or after more practice.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: Agreed. We can describe what happened without presenting it as a stable pattern across everyone's study routine.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Is using paper for the planning sheet itself a limitation?

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: Not if the records were legible and complete.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: And the session did take place, so cancellation isn't relevant.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Exactly. A limitation should explain why the evidence may support a narrower claim, rather than simply list practical details that make the project look less impressive.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What is the second limitation?

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: The tasks used in the two rounds differed in difficulty. We changed the planning method and also gave participants less familiar material in the second round.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Yes, so a difference in completion cannot be attributed only to the new plan.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What would you do next?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Use more comparable tasks or explain the remaining differences clearly.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: We should also preserve the pilot records rather than rewrite the plan as though we had controlled task difficulty from the start.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then your two limitations are one afternoon and unequal task difficulty. The timer worked and the room was available, so neither is another obstacle in this pilot.

parts.title: Investigating how study time is used

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Consider a fictional study of how a small student group uses a limited working period. The first stage defines the goal of the task. A goal should describe the required result, not merely the intention to work hard or remain busy. In this example, the task requires a comparison and a short recommendation, so both belong in the definition. If the group measures only the length of the final response, it may reward extra writing that does not fulfil the instruction. Defining the goal before observing work helps the team decide what successful completion means and prevents an attractive but incomplete product from silently replacing the result the task actually requested.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The second stage records a baseline using the group's existing approach. The baseline provides a starting record against which a later attempt can be described. It should include the task conditions and any obvious interruption, rather than present the first attempt as though it occurred in an empty, perfectly controlled setting. The group does not need to invent a sophisticated tracking system for this stage. It needs a clear account of what was done and when major stages began. A baseline is useful because its meaning can be examined later, not because the first observed session automatically represents every occasion on which the students work.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The third stage groups recorded activity into categories. The team agrees what counts as reading requirements, planning, producing the response and checking it. A category should describe an observable stage without requiring the observer to guess how deeply somebody was thinking. Some actions may serve more than one purpose, so the team records a rule for ambiguous cases. These categories make comparison possible only if they are applied consistently. A detailed chart can still mislead when one observer classifies rereading as checking and another classifies the same action as planning. The point of the categories is shared meaning, not simply a more colourful display of the session.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fourth stage plans a buffer for uncertainty in the next attempt. A buffer is reserved time that has not already been promised to another stage. It can absorb a small unexpected delay without forcing the group to abandon every remaining requirement. The size of the reserve should relate to the task and the uncertainty the group has identified. Calling a period a buffer does not make it available twice. If participants spend it on an early section, it is no longer waiting at the end. The planning record should show when the reserve was used and what problem it addressed, so the review can assess whether it served a useful purpose.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fifth stage conducts a review comparing the plan with the completed work. The review considers both the allocation and whether the required outputs are present. A participant may follow the timetable exactly while misunderstanding the task, or depart from the timetable for a well-explained reason and still produce a complete response. Those situations should not receive the same interpretation. The team asks which decision helped, which created difficulty and what evidence supports that judgement. A useful review preserves the distinction between a procedure that was followed and a procedure that worked for the intended goal. The two can coincide, but one does not automatically prove the other.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Interruptions should be recorded with enough context to interpret them. An interruption may be external, such as an announcement, or arise from the participant deciding to check an unrelated message. These events can affect available working time, but they should not all be treated as evidence of the same planning problem. The team needs to distinguish an unavoidable condition from a choice that might be changed in a later attempt. It should also avoid collecting unnecessary details about the message or the person involved. The useful information concerns how the task was interrupted and how the participant resumed it, not a complete account of everything happening around the student.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Switching between tasks can also complicate the record. A person may move from reading to writing and back because the task requires it, rather than because the plan failed. The team should describe the transitions before judging them. Some switching may be purposeful, while repeated movement caused by a forgotten requirement may reveal a different issue. A simple count of transitions cannot distinguish those explanations on its own. The review can use the participant's account alongside the observation, while keeping the two sources separate. The aim is to understand whether a transition supported the task, not to assume that uninterrupted activity is always the best use of time.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Fatigue is another possible influence on performance during a session. If the later task follows several demanding activities, a change in completion may reflect more than the planning method being tested. The team should describe the sequence and allow its interpretation to remain qualified. It cannot establish the effect of fatigue merely by noticing that somebody looked tired. A short account of the conditions may help identify a question for a better-designed later study. This is one reason a small pilot should not produce a universal recommendation about the ideal number of minutes for every stage. The observed result belongs to a particular task, group and sequence of activities.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Time estimates should include uncertainty. A prediction of exactly twelve minutes can look more authoritative than the information behind it justifies. The group may find it more useful to state an expected range and explain which features could make the stage take longer. A range is not permission to ignore the overall limit. It is a way to recognise variability while deciding where a reserve or an early check would be helpful. The review should compare the estimate with what happened and examine the reason for a difference. Replacing one overly precise guess with another after each attempt would not by itself improve the group's understanding of the work.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Finally, the team considers transfer to other tasks. A routine that helped with a familiar short comparison may need adjustment for a longer task with new information or a different required output. The stage review records the conditions under which the routine appeared useful and identifies what should be tested next. It should not advertise one successful attempt as proof that the same timetable will work everywhere. Transfer is a question about what carries across and what must change. By making that question explicit, the group can preserve a useful principle, such as checking required outputs, while adapting the allocation to the actual demands of the next task.
